title: The Corpus Christi hymns (1264)
hook: the pope asks Thomas to write the texts for the new feast

segments.voice: Yesterday, substance: what a thing is, beneath how it looks, and Thomas's account of the change at Mass. Your line was what it is, not how it looks. Who did you look at twice? Day one thousand one hundred eighty.
screen: `WHAT IT IS, NOT HOW IT LOOKS.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was hard thinking: substance, accidents, a change that moves nothing. Pages of careful argument. Today the same man is handed a different job. Tradition says Pope Urban the Fourth, setting up a new feast for the Body of Christ, asked Thomas Aquinas to write its texts: the prayers, the antiphons, the hymns to be sung. So the professor who wrote the Summa sits down to write songs. And the songs he's credited with are still sung at Benediction, at processions, on Holy Thursday night. Today: what happens when a theologian has to make it rhyme.
screen: `PAGES OF CAREFUL ARGUMENT.` → `A NEW FEAST NEEDS HYMNS.` → `THE PROFESSOR WRITES SONGS.`

segments.voice: Start with the first line of the Pange lingua: "Pange, lingua, gloriosi Corporis mysterium." Sing, my tongue, the mystery of the glorious body. Those first three words weren't new. An older hymn of the cross, by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, opens with the same three: Pange, lingua, gloriosi. Thomas takes the old opening and turns it from the cross to the altar. The cross and the Eucharist, in one echo. Then listen to what he does with yesterday's lesson. In the fourth verse he writes: "Verbum caro, panem verum verbo carnem efficit." The Word made flesh, by his word, makes true bread into flesh. Word and flesh, flesh and word, chasing each other across one line. The incarnation and the Eucharist, folded into wordplay a choir can sing. The same verse goes on: even if the senses fail, faith alone is enough to steady a sincere heart. And the hymn's last two verses, sung on their own, became the Tantum ergo: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui." So great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. A few lines later comes this: "Praestet fides supplementum sensuum defectui." Let faith supply what the senses lack. It's yesterday's question about bread that still tastes like bread, answered not in an argument but in a song. The Summa works it out over pages. The hymn gives it to a choir to sing. Same man, same truth, two ways of holding it.
screen: `SING, MY TONGUE: AN OLD OPENING.` · `WORD AND FLESH IN ONE LINE.` · `TANTUM ERGO: SO GREAT A SACRAMENT.` · `FAITH SUPPLIES WHAT THE SENSES LACK.` · then, large: `PANGE, LINGUA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or read the Pange lingua. Take one easy breath first. If you know the tune of the Tantum ergo, sing it softly, even just the first two lines. If you don't, read them slowly in Latin, one word per breath: Tantum. Ergo. Sacramentum. Veneremur. Cernui. Then the English sense: so great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. If you pray, let it be your prayer. If you don't, simply notice what it's like to say an old line slowly. The bell holds the time.
The Corpus Christi hymns. The songs tradition credits to Thomas for the feast of the Body of Christ: the Pange lingua, with its Tantum ergo, and others. Today's word.
Your line: sing, my tongue. Today, take one thing you believe or love and hum it, say it aloud, or sing it, instead of only thinking it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Catholics sing the Tantum ergo at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, and the Pange lingua accompanies the procession of the Eucharist at the end of the Holy Thursday Mass and on the feast of Corpus Christi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a theologian's hymns would be dry.
what it means: the hymns sing the same truth as the Summa: the Word made flesh, faith supplying what the senses lack.
what a scholar hears: Thomas borrows his opening from Fortunatus's hymn of the cross, and verbum caro plays word against flesh.

notes: Latin wording to confirm against the Roman Breviary: Pange lingua v. 1 and v. 4, Tantum ergo lines 1–2 and 5–6. English glosses are the writer's plain renderings, not a published translation.
Authorship and the papal commission are given as tradition ('tradition says', 'credited'); no year is stated in the voice (the index title carries 1264).

Day 672 already told the feast's history (Juliana of Liège, the procession, the monstrance); this day stays inside the hymn texts to avoid repeating it. Day 681 quoted Fortunatus's 'Crux fidelis'; this day only notes the shared opening.
Tantum ergo as the final two verses of Pange lingua, sung at Benediction; the Pange lingua at the Holy Thursday transfer of the Eucharist and Corpus Christi processions (howItsDone). Confirm.

Editor pass: removed the superlative 'hardest kind of thinking' and the overclaim 'the whole doctrine'; replaced the explains/kneels ending, which day 1181 uses as its central image; varied the practice opener.
